note.title: Calculating combined resistance
note.subject: science

mustKnow: Two equal resistors in parallel: R = R1 ÷ 2
Higher: any two in parallel, 1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2 (then invert); check with R = R1 × R2 ÷ (R1 + R2)
Higher: a circuit with series and parallel sections: reduce the parallel section first, then add

notOnThisSpec: Three or more resistors all in parallel, and the rule for n equal resistors
Potential dividers, resistivity (R = ρL / A) and internal resistance
Potential difference as the required word (CCEA says voltage)

mustBeAbleTo: Calculate the total resistance of resistors in series by adding
Calculate the resistance of two equal resistors in parallel by halving one
Explain why adding a resistor in parallel lowers the total resistance
Higher: calculate the combined resistance of any two resistors in parallel with 1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2, inverting at the end
Higher: reduce a circuit with series and parallel sections to one resistance, parallel section first
Work out the resistance between two points when switches open a branch or bypass a resistor
Choose an arrangement of given resistors that reaches a stated total
Use a total resistance with V = I R to find a current
sheet.howExamined: P2, 1 hour 15 minutes, 70 marks at Foundation and 80 at Higher, calculator allowed. Foundation sets one-mark totals: resistors in series, an equal pair in parallel (Summer 2019 Q5(a), 2022 Q4(c), 2025 Q4(c)), and a resistor feeding an equal pair using the earlier answer (2021 Q5(a)). Higher sets 1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2 for three marks (equation, substitution, answer: 2021 Q7(a)(i)), a switch table (2021 Q7(a)(ii)), arrangements of three given resistors for four totals (2019 Q5(b), 2023 Q6(a)), then currents and V = I R on the same circuit.
traps: Adding two equal resistors that are in parallel: halve one; a parallel total is less than either resistor (Summer 2025 P2 Foundation Q4)
Stopping at 1/R, adding an unequal pair, or halving its sum: invert the reciprocal sum and check it is below the smaller resistor (Summer 2023 P2 Higher Q6)
Adding every resistor in a circuit with a parallel section: reduce the pair first, then add along the line (Summer 2023 P2 Higher Q6)
Using a total resistance in a wrong form of V = I R: I = V ÷ R, never R ÷ V (Summer 2024 P2 Foundation Q7, Higher Q4)

steps.working: B and C are an equal pair in parallel: 16 ÷ 2 = 8 Ω.
steps.decision: Deal with the parallel pair first, and notice it is an equal pair, so the Foundation shortcut applies: half of one.

options: Because two equal routes carry twice the current of one, so the pair has half the resistance
Because the 16 Ω is shared between B and C
Because every parallel pair is halved, whatever the two resistances
whyMenu.explain: Twice the route for the same voltage means twice the current, so half the resistance. The halving works only because B and C are equal; an unequal pair needs the Higher equation.

steps.working: A is in series with the pair: 16 + 8 = 24 Ω.
steps.decision: Now the circuit is one line: A, then the single resistor that replaced the pair. Series resistances add.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: B and C together: 8 Ω; between P and R: 24 Ω.

steps.decision: Parallel section first. Product over sum is quickest for two resistors; the reciprocal equation gives the same.

options: Because the series resistor can only be added once the pair is a single value
Because parallel resistors are always larger
Because the battery is next to the pair
whyMenu.explain: Adding along a line needs every piece of the line as one value. The pair becomes one resistor first; then the circuit is a simple series line.

steps.decision: The battery sees the total resistance: V = I R rearranged for I.

items.stem: Before we start (from the series and parallel rules): in a series circuit, how does the current through one resistor compare with the current through another?

options.text: it is the same
options.feedback: Yes. One loop, one current.

options.text: it is smaller after each resistor
options.feedback: Resistors do not use current up: the same current passes every point of a series loop.

options.text: it is larger through the smaller resistor
options.feedback: That is true of parallel branches. In series there is one route, so one current.

items.stem: Before we start (from the series and parallel rules): in a parallel circuit, what is the voltage across each branch?

options.text: the supply voltage
options.feedback: Yes. Each branch is joined straight across the supply.

options.text: the supply voltage shared between the branches
options.feedback: Sharing belongs to series. Each parallel branch has the whole supply voltage.

options.text: it depends only on the current in that branch
options.feedback: Each branch is joined straight across the supply, so its voltage is the supply voltage whatever current it carries.

items.stem: Before we start (from Ohm's law): a 12 V supply is connected across an 8 Ω resistor. What current flows?

options.feedback: That divides the resistance by the voltage. I = V ÷ R = 12 ÷ 8 = 1.5 A.
That multiplies. I = V ÷ R = 12 ÷ 8 = 1.5 A.

items.stem: Before we start (from Mathematics): what is 1/4 + 1/12?
items.skill: Prerequisite: adding fractions with a common denominator

options.feedback: Adding tops and bottoms is not how fractions add. Use a common denominator: 3/12 + 1/12 = 4/12 = 1/3.
That multiplies the fractions. Adding them over twelfths gives 3/12 + 1/12 = 1/3.

items.stem: Resistors of 3 Ω, 9 Ω and 18 Ω are connected in series. What is the total resistance?

options.feedback: That is only the largest resistor. In series every resistance adds: 30 Ω.
That averages the smallest and largest. In series every resistance adds: 3 + 9 + 18 = 30 Ω.

items.stem: Two 30 Ω resistors are connected in parallel. What is their combined resistance?
items.skill: Two equal in parallel: halve one

options.feedback: That adds them, the series rule. Side by side, halve one: 15 Ω.
A second route lowers the total below one resistor: 30 ÷ 2 = 15 Ω.

items.stem: (Higher) A 10 Ω and a 15 Ω resistor are connected in parallel. What is their combined resistance?

options.text: 6 Ω

options.feedback: That adds them. A parallel total is less than the smaller resistor: 6 Ω.
Halving the sum only works for an equal pair: 6 Ω.
That is 1/R. Turn it upside down: R = 30 ÷ 5 = 6 Ω.

items.stem: (Higher) A 2 Ω resistor is in series with a 6 Ω and a 3 Ω resistor that are in parallel with each other. What is the total resistance?

options.text: 4 Ω
options.feedback: Yes: the pair is 6 × 3 ÷ 9 = 2 Ω; add 2 Ω: 4 Ω.
That adds all three. Reduce the pair first (2 Ω), then add: 4 Ω.
The pair went in as 1/R. Invert it first, 2 Ω, then add: 4 Ω.

items.stem: A resistor is connected in parallel with a lamp that is already lit by a battery. What happens to the current from the battery?

options.text: it increases, because the total resistance has fallen
options.feedback: Yes. The resistor is another route with the full battery voltage across it, so the battery supplies extra current.

options.text: it decreases, because there is more resistance in the circuit
options.feedback: Side by side, a new resistor is a new route, so the total resistance falls and the current rises.

options.text: it stays the same, because the battery is the same
options.feedback: The new branch carries extra current for the same voltage, so the battery supplies more current in total.

items.stem: A closed switch is connected directly across one resistor in a series circuit. What does that resistor now add to the total resistance?

options.text: nothing: the current goes round it through the switch
options.feedback: Yes. The closed switch is a path with almost no resistance, so the current bypasses the resistor.

options.text: its full resistance, as before
options.feedback: The closed switch gives the current a path round the resistor, so the resistor no longer adds to the total.

options.text: half its resistance, because it is now in parallel with the switch
options.feedback: The switch is a path with almost no resistance, so it takes all the current and the resistor adds nothing.

parts.stem: A resistor is added in series with the resistors already in a circuit. What happens to the total resistance?

options.text: it increases
options.feedback: Yes. Another resistor on the one route adds its own opposition.

options.text: it decreases
options.feedback: That is what a resistor added in parallel does. In series the new resistor lies on the only route, so the total goes up.

options.text: it stays the same, because the supply is the same
options.feedback: The supply does not set the resistance. A resistor added in series adds its value to the total.

parts.workedSolution: It increases: in series every resistance adds to the total.

hints: Think of the new branch as a second route for the charge.
parts.stem: A resistor is added in parallel with a resistor already in a circuit. What happens to the total resistance?

options.text: it decreases
options.feedback: Yes. A new branch is another route, so more current flows for the same voltage and the total resistance falls.

options.text: it increases, because there is more resistance in the circuit
options.feedback: More resistors does not mean more resistance when they are side by side. The new branch is another route for the charge, so the total falls.

options.text: it stays the same, because each branch has the same voltage
options.feedback: The voltage across each branch does stay the same, but the new branch carries extra current, so the total resistance falls.

parts.workedSolution: It decreases: the new branch gives the charge another route, so more current flows for the same voltage.

hints: Compare each choice with the smaller of the two resistors.
parts.stem: A 30 Ω and a 60 Ω resistor are connected in parallel. Which of these could be their combined resistance?

options.feedback: Yes. A parallel total is less than the smaller resistor, and only 20 Ω is below 30 Ω.
That is half their sum, the shortcut for an equal pair. These are not equal, and a parallel total must be less than 30 Ω.
That is the series total. Side by side, the total must be less than the smaller resistor, 30 Ω.

parts.workedSolution: 20 Ω: two resistors in parallel always combine to less than the smaller one, 30 Ω. (Higher: 1/R = 1/30 + 1/60 = 3/60, R = 20 Ω.)

scheme.examinerNote: A point about the meters counts only when the right meter is in the right place: an ammeter across the resistors, or a voltmeter in series, earns nothing. The explanation needs the idea of an extra route for the current; 'more resistors so more resistance' is the misconception the question tests and earns nothing.

parts.workedSolution: Connect one resistor to the battery with the ammeter in series, in the main line, and the voltmeter in parallel across the resistor. Read the voltage and the current and find the resistance from R = V / I. Then connect a second resistor in parallel with the first, keeping the voltmeter across the pair and the ammeter in the main line, and take the readings again. With the second resistor added the current is larger for the same voltage, so the combined resistance is smaller, less than either resistor on its own, and it can be checked against 1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2. This happens because the second resistor gives the current another path. Keep the current small and switch off between readings so the resistors do not heat up.

Orla is asked: 'Two 16 Ω resistors are connected in parallel. Calculate their total resistance. [1]'
Her answer:
studentWorking: The two resistors are in parallel
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Adding is the series rule. Two equal resistors side by side are two equal routes, so the pair has half the resistance of one: 16 ÷ 2 = 8 Ω. A parallel total bigger than either resistor is always a warning sign.
findTheMistake.feedback: No mark as written: the pair is in parallel, so the answer is 8 Ω, not 32 Ω. Summer 2025 Foundation examiners saw exactly this.

Ruairi is asked: 'A 20 Ω and a 5 Ω resistor are connected in parallel. Calculate their combined resistance. [3]'
His answer:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: The sum on line 3 is 1/R, not R. The last step turns it upside down: R = 1 ÷ 0.25 = 4 Ω. Check: 4 Ω is less than 5 Ω, the smaller resistor, while 0.25 Ω is far too small to be right.
findTheMistake.feedback: Two marks of three: the equation and the substitution are right. The answer mark needs the reciprocal inverted, 4 Ω, the step the Summer 2023 Higher examiners found much less well known.

Sinéad is asked: 'A 12.0 V battery is connected to an 8 Ω resistor in series with a 6 Ω and a 3 Ω resistor in parallel. Calculate the current from the battery. [5]'
Her answer:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: V = I R rearranges to I = V ÷ R, voltage over resistance. Line 3 turns it the wrong way up. I = 12.0 ÷ 10 = 1.2 A.
findTheMistake.feedback: Three marks of five: the resistance work is right. An incorrect form of the equation scores nothing for the current, as Summer 2024 Foundation examiners saw: I = V ÷ R = 1.2 A.

prompts.answer: Half of one of them: R = R1 ÷ 2.

prompts.prompt: (Higher) What equation gives the combined resistance of any two resistors in parallel?
prompts.answer: 1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2, then turn the answer upside down.

prompts.prompt: Two resistors are in parallel. How does their combined resistance compare with the smaller one?
prompts.answer: It is always smaller than the smaller resistor.

prompts.prompt: (Higher) A circuit has a series part and a parallel part. Which do you work out first?
prompts.answer: The parallel part; then add the series resistors.

prompts.prompt: (Higher) What is the quick check for two resistors in parallel?
prompts.answer: Multiply them and divide by their sum: R = R1 × R2 ÷ (R1 + R2).

prompts.prompt: A closed switch is connected across a resistor. What does that resistor add to the total?
prompts.answer: Nothing: the current goes round it through the switch.

prompts.prompt: Why does adding a resistor in parallel lower the total resistance?
prompts.answer: It gives the current another route, so more current flows for the same voltage.
